title: Delays, behaviour and transmission: modelling the impact of effective private provider engagement on tuberculosis control in urban India
abstract: Abstract In India, the country with the world’s largest burden of tuberculosis (TB), most patients first seek care in the private healthcare sector, which is fragmented and unregulated. Ongoing initiatives are demonstrating effective approaches for engaging with this sector, and form a central part of India’s recent National Strategic Plan: here we aimed to address their potential impact on TB transmission in urban settings, when taken to scale. We developed a mathematical model of TB transmission dynamics, calibrated to urban populations in Mumbai and Patna, two major cities in India where pilot interventions are currently ongoing. We found that, when taken to sufficient scale to capture 75% of patient-provider interactions, the intervention could reduce incidence by upto 21.3% (95% Bayesian credible interval (CrI) 13.0 – 32.5%) and 15.8% (95% CrI 7.8 – 28.2%) in Mumbai and Patna respectively, between 2018 and 2025. There is a stronger impact on TB mortality, with a reduction of up to 38.1% (95% CrI 20.0 – 55.1%) in the example of Mumbai. The incidence impact of this intervention alone may be limited by the amount of transmission that has already occurred by the time a patient first presents for care: model estimates suggest an initial patient delay of 4-5 months before first seeking care, followed by a diagnostic delay of 1-2 months before ultimately initiating TB treatment. Our results suggest that the transmission impact of such interventions could be maximised by additional measures to encourage early uptake of TB services.

summary.oneLiner: A TB transmission model suggests engaging private providers in Mumbai and Patna could cut incidence by about 16-21%, but early care-seeking is a key limit.
summary.overview: Most Indian TB patients first go to private providers, which are fragmented and often do not diagnose TB accurately. The authors built a mathematical model of TB spread calibrated to Mumbai and Patna and simulated scaling up a public-private support programme (PPSA) that subsidises good diagnosis and adherence support. They estimate it could reduce TB incidence by up to about 21% in Mumbai and 16% in Patna between 2018 and 2025, with a larger effect on deaths. However, the model suggests that transmission before patients first seek care limits the incidence impact, so measures to encourage earlier care-seeking may be needed alongside it.
summary.question: What impact could effective engagement of private TB providers, through a PPSA model, have on TB transmission and incidence in urban India, and what are the key drivers of that impact?
summary.method: A deterministic compartmental transmission model of TB with patient and provider pathways, calibrated to prevalence, annual risk of TB infection and drug-resistance data. Pathway parameters were estimated from community patient-pathway surveys using an Expectation-Maximisation algorithm, and uncertainty was propagated with Bayesian melding. Sensitivity analyses used partial rank correlation coefficients and scenario tests on infectivity and provider quality.
summary.data: Community-based patient pathway surveys in Mumbai (76 TB patients, 196 patient-provider interactions) and Patna (64 TB patients, 121 interactions). Calibration targets were borrowed from a Chennai prevalence survey and Chennai/Delhi infection surveys, plus program-reported drug-resistance data for Mumbai and national-average assumptions for Patna. Simulated period 2018 to 2025.
findings: At 75% coverage of patient-provider interactions, the intervention could reduce incidence by up to 21.3% (95% CrI 13.0-32.5%) in Mumbai and 15.8% (95% CrI 7.8-28.2%) in Patna, 2018-2025.
Mortality impact in Mumbai is stronger, with a reduction of up to 38.1% (95% CrI 20.0-55.1%) in the timely diagnosis scenario.
The incidence impact of the intervention alone may be limited by transmission that has already occurred before a patient first presents for care.
Model estimates suggest an initial patient delay of about 4.4 months in Mumbai and 5.2 months in Patna, with broad uncertainty; the authors note this is inferred, not directly measured.
Prevalence and annual risk of TB infection were the inputs most influencing the simulated impact.
In Mumbai, quality of diagnosis and treatment among less-than-fully-qualified providers appears key; in Patna, quality among fully qualified providers appears most important.
The authors suggest the transmission impact could be maximised by additional measures to encourage early uptake of TB services.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest private sector engagement is a key foundation for TB control in India but will not alone meet elimination aspirations. Intervention priorities may need tailoring by city, and measures that shorten patient delay (such as active case-finding or demand generation) could increase impact. The paper is a preprint and its patient-delay finding is model-inferred rather than directly measured.
